questions.question: Your Go web server gets 10,000 concurrent requests — how does it handle them without 10,000 OS threads?
questions.title: Goroutine Vs Thread Scenario
questions.direct_answer: One goroutine per connection (~2KB each = ~20MB for 10k) — Go's scheduler multiplexes them onto GOMAXPROCS OS threads (cores). Requests that block on I/O park their goroutine (the thread moves on); computation runs in parallel across cores.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: One goroutine per connection (~2KB each = ~20MB for 10k) — Go's scheduler multiplexes them onto GOMAXPROCS OS threads (cores). Requests that block on I/O park their goroutine (the thread moves on); computation runs in parallel across cores.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R[10000 requests] --> G[10000 goroutines ~20MB]
    G --> P[16 Ps = 16 cores]
    P --> M[16 OS threads RUNNING]
    G --> BLOCKED[most goroutines: parked on I/O]
    BLOCKED --> POLL[netpoller wakes when data arrives]
    POLL --> P
    DB[downstream: DB pool max 25 + queue]
    FD[file descriptors: ulimit]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The scenario's three states per goroutine, and where they live:
- RUNNING (on a thread) — 16 at a time (GOMAXPROCS)
- RUNNABLE (in a P's queue) — waiting for a free thread
- BLOCKED (parked) — on the network poller (I/O), on a channel, on a mutex, on a timer

The 10,000-request distribution: at any instant, ~16 RUNNING (the cores), most BLOCKED (waiting on the DB/downstream), a few RUNNABLE (just-woken responses). The scheduler's work: wake the right goroutines when their I/O completes (the netpoller's event loop) — the efficiency that makes this model work.

The GOMAXPROCS question (the follow-up): more Ps than cores doesn't help (the cores are the parallelism ceiling); fewer Ps than cores underuses (deliberate throttling — the container-aware GOMAXPROCS story, where Go 1.25 reads cgroup CPU limits — the kernel scheduling composes with Go's).
